frase_gancho.texto: A green stone face with no age and no name.

puente_narrativo.texto: The dead take their leave with a face of stone; the living call down the rain with a sound. Listen with your imagination: it comes from stone conch shells with feathers, on a palace wall.

guion_corto.texto: This green stone mask, made of polished serpentine, is a funerary face from Teotihuacán. Look at its features: a broad, smooth forehead, a straight nose, marked eyelids, a slightly open mouth. It is not anyone’s portrait. The people of Teotihuacán preferred faces without age and without expression, as if the deceased left their identity behind to become part of the divine world. For them, green stone was the color of water, of plants and of maize, that is, of life. To place it beside a dead person was to give them a face that does not grow old. Centuries later, the Mexica searched for objects like this one among the ruins and kept them as relics, because they came from the city of the gods.

guion_largo.texto:
Observe it calmly. The forehead is broad and smooth, the nose runs straight down from the forehead, and the ears are rectangles with perforations where shell ear ornaments may once have hung. The mouth is slightly open, as in a last breath. On other masks of this style, the eyes have inlays of shell and obsidian that give them a fixed gaze. Everything is so balanced that it looks like any face and no face.

Serpentine takes its name from its mottled look, like snakeskin. It is a softer stone than jade, but it can be polished until it shines a deep green. Carving it without metal tools demanded a great deal of time, with sand, water and patience. And all that work was for an object that perhaps no one would ever see again: it went with a dead person or in an offering, underground, where no living person would see it. That generosity says a lot about how much the afterlife mattered.

What were these masks for? It is an open question. Many have been found not on a body but in offerings, and we do not know whether they covered the face of a funerary bundle or whether they were gifts for the gods. Some have edges and perforations that suggest they were attached to something. However it may be, they put a permanent face where the body was going to fade away.

Green was the most valuable color in Mesoamerica. Jade, serpentine and quetzal feathers were worth more than gold, and they were associated with water, young maize and life. In the Maya Hall you will see how that idea reaches its extreme: the [jade mask of Pakal](mna_s09_mascara_pakal), a king covered with a green mosaic for his journey to the afterlife. This one from Teotihuacán is a simple ancestor of that mask.

The Mexica felt enormous reverence for Teotihuacán. They dug into its ruins, took away objects and buried them again in their own temples: in the offerings of the Templo Mayor, objects in the Teotihuacán style appeared that they kept for centuries. For the Mexica, that city was the place where the Sun and the Moon had been born. It was their sacred past, and a mask like this one, a relic.

This face reminds us of something you saw from the first hall: the body as a canvas. Deformed skulls, filed teeth, face paint, ear ornaments: people transformed their bodies to say who they were. Here the opposite happens. The individual is erased to leave only a divine face, without wrinkles, without age, without personal history.

Teotihuacán was also a city of many origins. In a neighborhood to the west lived people who had come from Oaxaca, who kept making pottery and performing rituals in their own way; other neighborhoods had workshops for obsidian, for shell, for green stone. But in the face of death, and before a mask like this one, everyone became, in a certain way, equal.

Look one last time at the slightly open mouth. It seems about to say something. And in a certain way it did: centuries later, those who found it understood that it came from a place of gods.

texto.Material: Dark green serpentine, carved and burnished
texto.Dimensions: 21 cm high x 20 cm wide x 10.5 cm thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: Funerary masks were portraits of the deceased.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The people of Teotihuacán preferred idealized, ageless faces; the mask does not copy a person, it represents their transformation.
